overview: The Xia is the first dynasty in Chinese tradition, associated by most Chinese scholars with the Erlitou archaeological culture of the middle Yellow River valley. Whether it was a historical state or a later political myth remains debated outside China, but the material culture of the period shows the first large-scale bronze production and palace architecture in the region.

items.text: Erlitou casts the earliest Chinese bronze ritual vessels, small jue wine cups, in sectioned clay moulds, the piece-mould method the Shang would carry to its height.
Flood control and irrigation works are attributed by tradition to the founder Yu the Great; the story is legend, but the Yellow River floodplain was being farmed and managed in this period.
Plain bronze jue and jade blades, sceptres and cong tubes from Erlitou set the forms that later dynasties elaborated and decorated.
Turquoise-inlaid bronze plaques with animal designs, and a dragon of some two thousand turquoise pieces laid on a body in an Erlitou tomb.
Ancestor offerings and divination with burnt animal bones appear in the archaeological record, anticipating Shang and Zhou religion.
The legend of Yu controlling the floods established the model of the virtuous ruler who brings order from chaos.
Millet farming and pig husbandry supported growing populations in the Yellow River valley.
Rammed-earth foundations and walls enclosed the palace compound at Erlitou, a walled precinct of about eleven hectares.
In the traditional histories the cycle of dynasties begins with the Xia: Tang of Shang overthrows its last king, and the Zhou later name the pattern the Mandate of Heaven.
The name Xia later became synonymous with Chinese civilization itself, in the word Huaxia.

fall.text: According to tradition, the tyrant Jie was defeated by Tang of Shang at the Battle of Mingtiao.

sources.title: Michael Loewe and Edward L. Shaughnessy (eds.), The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999), chapter 3, Erlitou
